projects.title: trey-lm
projects.summary: A portfolio site whose chat model shows how it picks every word.
projects.outcome: A live model that answers questions about Trey while visitors watch its neurons, attention and next-word odds.
projects.html:
trey-lm is the language model on Trey's portfolio site. It runs Llama 3.2 3B Instruct and answers questions about Trey using only his notes, which are retrieved with Supermemory and placed into the prompt.

While it writes, the page shows what happens inside: 28 layers drawn as towers of windows, the five most likely next words, which parts of the prompt it is looking at, and what earlier layers would have guessed. Trey built the visualizer, the streaming backend, and the animated Cincinnati skyline behind it.

projects.title: Victor Hacks memory archive
projects.summary: Overall winner at Victor Hacks (April 2026). A cryptographically secured archive for preserving and sharing loved ones' memories.
projects.outcome: Overall winner of the Victor Hacks hackathon, April 2026.
projects.html:
In April 2026, Trey McGonnell and his team won the overall prize at the Victor Hacks hackathon.

Together they built a cryptographically secured memory archive: a place to preserve and share the memories of loved ones. The project was built with Python, MongoDB and TypeScript, and connected several AI and blockchain services: Gemini 2.5, ElevenLabs, Featherless AI and Solana.

projects.title: Evolutionary Algorithms in Machine Learning
projects.summary: A research paper on how genetic algorithms work and where they are used, from NASA's evolved antenna to real-time computer vision.
projects.outcome: Final research paper for Introduction to Data Science (DSC 101) at NKU, December 2025.
projects.html:
Overview

In the fall of 2025 (September to December), Trey McGonnell wrote a research paper titled "Evolutionary Algorithms in Machine Learning and Applications" for his Introduction to Data Science course (DSC 101) at Northern Kentucky University. The paper explains how evolutionary algorithms and genetic algorithms work and where they are used today. Trey wrote it for beginners with only a basic understanding of artificial intelligence, so it explains the ideas without heavy math.

Before writing, Trey built an annotated bibliography of about a dozen sources, including peer-reviewed papers, a NASA paper, a survey from the Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand, and explainer articles and videos.

How genetic algorithms work

Trey's paper explains that genetic algorithms are modeled on Darwin's idea of natural selection. A genetic algorithm starts with a random population of candidate solutions. Each candidate gets a fitness score that measures how good it is. The weakest candidates are removed, and new "offspring" are made by combining parts of two surviving parents (crossover). Each offspring then has a chance of a random change (mutation). Mutation matters because it helps the search explore new options and keeps it from getting stuck in a local optimum. The cycle repeats each generation until the algorithm reaches a generation limit or a target fitness score.

The paper places these methods in context: genetic algorithms are a kind of evolutionary algorithm, which is a kind of machine learning, which is part of artificial intelligence. Evolutionary machine learning is used for feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, neural architecture search, clustering and classification. Its strengths include handling very large search spaces, running well on distributed computers, and working on both discrete and continuous optimization problems.

Applications Trey covered

NASA's evolved antenna (2006)

NASA engineers used a genetic algorithm to design a spacecraft antenna, hoping to beat a human-designed one. The algorithm built antennas from a tree of construction steps (move forward by a length and radius, rotate on the x, y and z axes) and scored each design on how well its radiation pattern matched the target. The evolved antenna reached 93% efficiency, compared with 38% for the human-designed antenna, and took about three person-months of work instead of five. NASA noted that the algorithm produced unusual designs an expert would be unlikely to come up with. It was NASA's first evolved hardware part.

Shortest routes: circuit boards and the traveling salesperson problem

Trey connected two problems that genetic algorithms solve in similar ways: laying out circuit boards (where wires can't cross and shorter distances make chips faster) and the traveling salesperson problem (visiting every city once with the shortest total distance). For both, the number of possible solutions grows so fast that checking them all is impossible for large cases. The 2024 study he reviewed used total distance as the fitness score (lower is better), tournament selection to choose parents, crossover at a random split point, and two mutations that flip or scramble the order of cities. The mutations kept the search from getting stuck, and the algorithm found optimized routes.

Real-time computer vision

Computer vision is one of Trey's personal interests. He reviewed a 2019 study that used a genetic algorithm to build lightweight image classifiers that can run on small embedded hardware instead of expensive deep learning models. Each candidate in the population was a sequence of image transformations (Gabor, Gaussian, Laplacian, median blur, Sobel and gradient filters) with their own settings. Each candidate was scored by training a random forest on the transformed images and measuring the percentage of images classified correctly. Tournament selection, crossover and mutation (changing parameters, the order of transformations, and how many there are) produced each new generation.

  • Classifying chicken eggs from candling images into good, cracked, dirty and fertilized: 99.1% accuracy, using 75% of the images for training and 25% for testing.
  • Retrained on road photos to classify dry, wet, snow, ice, puddle and sand conditions: 92% accuracy after 40 generations.

Trey highlighted that the same algorithm adapted to a completely new problem just by swapping the training images.

Conclusion

Trey's paper concludes that evolutionary algorithms can find patterns and designs that experts would not think of, and that the same core loop of population, fitness, selection, crossover and mutation adapts to very different problems: evolved hardware, route optimization and real-time image classification.

Main sources

  • Linden, Lohn and Hornby (2006), "Automated Antenna Design with Evolutionary Algorithms", NASA.
  • Linganathan and Singamsetty (2024), "Genetic algorithm to the bi-objective multiple travelling salesman problem", Alexandria Engineering Journal.
  • Guo, Zhang and Lee (2019), "Efficient evolutionary learning algorithm for real-time embedded vision applications", Electronics.
  • Al-Sahaf et al. (2019), "A survey on evolutionary machine learning", Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand.
  • AIMER Society, "Evolutionary algorithms in machine learning".
  • Brown (2016), "Evolutionary algorithms", Serious Science.

projects.title: Wal-Bot
projects.summary: A bot for the programming game Screeps that runs a Walmart-style market logistics operation to earn credits.
projects.html:
Wal-Bot is a bot Trey McGonnell is building for Screeps, a game made for programmers. In Screeps, players write code that runs around the clock and controls their colony in a shared world.

Wal-Bot takes a Walmart-style approach: instead of focusing on combat, it focuses on market logistics, moving and trading resources efficiently to earn credits.
